name: Democratic backsliding
scope: Democratic backsliding as the political-science literature defines it: the state-led debilitation or elimination of the political institutions that sustain an existing democracy (Bermeo, s1), which Lührmann and Lindberg place within the wider autocratization, any substantial decline of the core institutions of electoral democracy (s3). It covers the contemporary forms the scholarship names (promissory coups, executive aggrandizement, strategic electoral manipulation, elected governments subverting institutions from within, s1, s4) and the diagnosis of it as a threat. The sources split on terms (backsliding, erosion, decay, recession, deconsolidation, autocratization; s3, s5, s7) and on whether it describes only democracies or any regime (s2, s3); the audit takes the common core: weakening of free and fair elections, rights of speech, press and association, and the rule of law within a democracy. Because the sources define it as a process to be recognised and resisted, the positions recorded are those of its scholars on what democracy requires, as these sources state them. It excludes democratic breakdown by sudden coup (Linz) except as the contrast the sources draw, and country case studies except as examples.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: Levitsky and Ziblatt (end of Chapter 1) say democracies are not supposed to ban parties or prohibit candidates and that they do not advocate such measures; they put the filtering of extremists on mainstream parties instead.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Levitsky and Ziblatt (Introduction, Chapter 4) count the weakening of the courts and other neutral institutions as backsliding, even when a majority elected the leader doing it; Bermeo defines backsliding as state-led debilitation of the institutions that sustain democracy.

democracy-is-procedure.rationale: Lührmann and Lindberg define electoral democracy as clean elections together with freedom of association, universal suffrage, an elected executive and freedom of expression, and Levitsky and Ziblatt (Introduction) call a contest "free but not fair" when the government controls the media; elections alone are not enough.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Levitsky and Ziblatt (Chapter 1, Table 1; Chapter 4) treat suggesting that the constitution be suspended or basic rights restricted as a sign of authoritarian behaviour, and describe crises as the occasion autocrats use to dismantle checks.

one-party-rule.rationale: Lührmann and Lindberg define democracy by clean elections and freedom of association, and define autocratization as the decline of these requirements, so a party holding exclusive state leadership is the endpoint of backsliding that they study.

party-controls-media.rationale: Levitsky and Ziblatt (Chapter 1, Table 1; Chapter 4) treat curtailing the media and buying off or bullying it into silence as a mark of elected autocrats subverting democracy.

political-violence-legitimate.rationale: Levitsky and Ziblatt (Chapter 1, Table 1) make toleration or encouragement of violence one of four key indicators of authoritarian behaviour.

separated-powers.rationale: Levitsky and Ziblatt (Introduction and Chapter 4) treat checks and balances and the courts as the "institutional buffers" of democracy, and name packing and weaponizing them as how elected autocrats subvert it.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Levitsky and Ziblatt (Chapter 1, Table 1) list denying opponents' legitimacy and readiness to curtail the civil liberties of opponents among the warning signs of authoritarian behaviour, and cite Chavez jailing opposition figures (Introduction).

unlimited-reelection.rationale: Levitsky and Ziblatt (Introduction, Chapter 4) present eliminating presidential term limits so that Chavez could stay indefinitely, and Fujimori's effort to evade them, as steps in elected leaders' subversion of democracy.

summary: Democratic backsliding is the scholarly name for the weakening of an existing democracy, usually by its own elected leaders, through legal-looking steps that degrade free and fair elections, the courts, the press and the opposition's room to operate. The literature (Bermeo, Levitsky and Ziblatt, Lührmann and Lindberg) takes democratic institutions, norms of toleration and checks on executive power to be what must be defended.
